sentences.text: Nurhachius possessed an estimated wingspan ranging from 2.4 to 2.5 meters, while a separate calculation from 2008 by Witton suggested the span was 228 centimeters.
A separate calculation from 2008 by Witton suggested the span was 228 centimeters and the weight was 4 kilograms.
The skull featured a large nasoantorbital fenestra, an opening that occupied 58 percent of the skull length.
Measurements of the lower jaws indicated a length of 290 millimeters.
The teeth were robust, curved backward, and possessed three roots each.
These teeth were limited to the front of the jaws, totaling 54 individuals across both the upper and lower mandibles, with 28 in the upper jaw and 26 in the lower jaw.
The genus Nurhachius was named in 2005 by Wang Xiaolin, Alexander Kellner, Zhou Zhonghe, and Diogenes de Almeida Campos.
The genus name honors Nurhaci, the first emperor of the Qing Dynasty, whose power base included the fossil's discovery region.
The species name honors Ignácio Aureliano Machado Brito, a Brazilian paleontologist who pioneered pterosaur studies in his country.
The original description of Nurhachius was based on specimen IVPP V-13288, a partial skull and skeleton.
A second species, Nurhachius luei, was named in 2019.
Describers noted similarities with the Pteranodontoidea group, including a unique warped deltopectoral crest on the humerus shared with the Istiodactylus + Anhangueridae clade.
Cladistic analysis by Wang and colleagues placed Nurhachius within the family Istiodactylidae.
A 2008 analysis by Lü Junchang supported the close relationship between Nurhachius and Istiodactylus.
Zhou and colleagues confirmed the membership of Nurhachius in the family Istiodactylidae in 2019.
Nurhachius lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages of the Early Cretaceous in the Jiufotang Formation of Chaoyang, Liaoning, China.
Fossils of Nurhachius date back approximately 120 million years.
In 2008, Lü suggested that Nurhachius might be a junior synonym of Liaoxipterus.
A 2024 analysis by Hone et al. recovered the genus as paraphyletic, with N. luei being closer to Hongshanopterus.
